dataset_family: Lothian Birth Cohort 1936 (Edinburgh, Scotland): community birth cohort with MCI coded at wave 3 (age about 76) and wave 5 (age about 82); 292 have both codings
method_family: Longitudinal epidemiological cohort. Multinomial logistic regression of MCI transition categories (MCI stable, healthy-to-MCI, MCI-to-healthy) against a remained-cognitively-healthy reference, with ANOVA and chi-square group comparisons.
what_it_shows: Welstead et al., J Alzheimers Dis 80 (2021) 225-232. The PDF title, authors and DOI 10.3233/JAD-201282 match the block. Among 292 LBC1936 members, the depressive-symptom score is the HADS depression count; the PDF names the instrument, the block does not. Compared with those who stayed cognitively healthy (n = 215), each one-unit increase did not predict stable MCI (OR 1.15, p = 0.36, n = 20) or progression from healthy cognition to MCI (OR 1.01, p = 0.96, n = 36). It did predict reversion from MCI to healthy cognition (OR 1.37, p = 0.04, n = 21). People who progressed to dementia were excluded, and there are no brain measures.
why: NO. The Table A1 supporter sentence is about continuous severity scores failing to track brain measures or conversion, where conversion in context means MCI-to-dementia conversion (as in P-647 and P-26). P-932 has no brain measures and, by design, excludes participants who progressed to dementia. Its one significant depression result compares MCI reverters with people who were cognitively healthy at BOTH waves, not with MCI patients who stayed impaired. Every reverter had MCI at T1 and no member of the reference group did, so the OR largely restates a baseline status difference rather than testing prognosis within MCI. The within-MCI contrast (reverted vs stable MCI) is never run. Table 2 means are 2.47 vs 2.75, untested. The progression null (OR 1.01) is about incident MCI among cognitively healthy people. That is not MCI prognosis, and if anything it weighs against the row's first clause (depression status associated with MCI). A 'partly' reading would require treating incident MCI in healthy older adults as 'conversion' in the row's sense; I do not think the row supports that reading. The finders suggested a partial fit to 'the milder stratum sometimes carried the worse signal'. That phrase is in the ledger statement, not the Table A1 statement, and the paper's comparison does not show it within MCI. RELIABILITY. The reported statistics are internally inconsistent: (1) the post-hoc t(233) = 15.49 is implausible for means of 2.28 vs 2.75 with SDs near 2; (2) Table 3 prints the cardiovascular OR 3.13 under 'Transitioned healthy cognition to MCI', while the text assigns it to maintaining MCI; (3) the reverter mean/SD of 2.47 (1.96) duplicates the completer mean/SD of 2.47 [1.96]. Transition groups are small (20-36), as the authors acknowledge. INDEPENDENCE. LBC1936 is distinct from all current supporters (Korea Guro, Shanghai Brain Health, Shanghai Tongji, Florence) and from the other candidates. No shared authors. Not a preprint.

quotes.quote: Number of depressive symptoms were obtained from the Hospital Anxiety and Depression scale (HADS) [27].

Multinomial logistic regression models were ﬁt in order to assess the effect of various predictors on the likelihood of ﬁtting into one of three potential outcomes between T1 and T2 compared to the reference group of those who remained cognitively healthy.

Participants may have progressed to dementia over follow-up; however, they would then not have been eligible to take part in the next data wave, or if they did, they would be excluded from our analyses.
74% (n = 215) remained cognitively healthy, 7% (n = 20) remained MCI, 7% (n = 21) reverted from MCI to healthy cognition, and 12% (n = 36) transitioned to MCI.

those who remained cognitively healthy had signiﬁcantly fewer T1 depressive symptoms than those who remained MCI stable (t(233) = 15.49, p < 0.001), and those who reverted from MCI to healthy cognition (t(233) = 2.60, p < 0.01).
